opus-5.5.text:
I think they're really significant, and for a few reasons that go beyond the headline numbers.

First, they're a validation of the approach. When some of the most sophisticated drug discovery organizations in the world choose to work with you, it says they see AI-first drug design as something that can move real programs forward. These aren't small pilots. They involve hard targets that these companies care about.

Second, and this is what I find most exciting from the inside, they let us apply our technology to the full complexity of real drug discovery. It's one thing to build models that do well on benchmarks or predict structures accurately. It's another to take on a target that's resisted traditional approaches and try to design molecules with the right potency, selectivity, and properties. Partnerships put that pressure on the system, and that's where you learn the most. Every program teaches us something about where our models are strong and where we need to push further.

Third, there's a complementarity. Our partners bring decades of expertise in medicinal chemistry, clinical development, and getting medicines to patients. We bring a computational engine that we think can change how quickly and how creatively you explore chemical space. Putting those together is more powerful than either alone.

And alongside the partnerships, we're building our own internal pipeline. The two reinforce each other: partnered work tests the platform on a broad range of problems, and our internal programs let us pursue the full vision end to end. Ultimately, the measure of success isn't the deals themselves. It's whether this leads to better medicines reaching patients faster. The partnerships are an important step on that path.

r001.rationale: It says the partnerships are “not small pilots” and involve hard targets that have resisted traditional approaches, characterizing them as tests on entrenched problems.

r002.rationale: It describes applying technology to difficult targets, but does not say the models enabled new ways to modulate targets pursued for many years.

r003.rationale: It calls the partnerships a validation of the approach, but does not mention an expansion of the Novartis collaboration or treat such an expansion as evidence of success.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say those partnerships were significant on a few levels, and honestly the significance was a bit different from how it got reported at the time.

The headline numbers got a lot of attention, and sure, the economics matter. But what mattered more to us internally was validation of a thesis. When we started Isomorphic, the bet was that you could build a general-purpose AI drug discovery engine, not a one-disease, one-target shop. The question everyone asked was whether a company like ours could actually plug into the real pipeline of a big pharma, with all its chemistry and biology and clinical infrastructure, and add something they couldn't get elsewhere. Lilly and Novartis saying yes, and saying yes across multiple programs rather than a single pilot, was the industry telling us that the capabilities were real enough to put serious targets behind.

The second thing is what it did for the technology itself. These are hard problems. Some of the targets we've taken on are ones that have resisted conventional approaches for years. That pushes the models in a way that academic benchmarks never will. AlphaFold 3 and the generative chemistry work we've done since are better because they've been pointed at problems where the answer actually has to hold up in a wet lab, not just in a structure prediction metric.

And the third piece is more cultural. Partnering forced us to become a drug discovery company rather than an AI lab that happens to talk about drugs. You learn very quickly that a beautiful binding pose means nothing if the molecule can't be made, or has terrible pharmacokinetics, or hits something off-target. Having partners with decades of medicinal chemistry intuition in the room sharpened what we were building toward.

Now, I'd also be honest about what they don't yet prove. Partnerships are a leading indicator, not an outcome. The real test is clinical. A molecule in a human, showing the effect you predicted, with an acceptable safety profile. We've been clear that we want to see our own programs reach that stage, and I think the industry should hold all of us in this space to that standard rather than to deal announcements. But if you ask me whether those two partnerships moved the field forward, I think they did. They made it credible for pharma to think about AI as a core part of how you discover medicines rather than a tool you bolt on at the end.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts partnerships across multiple programs with a single pilot and says some targets had resisted conventional approaches for years, framing the work as testing the technology on entrenched problems.

r002.rationale: It says the partnerships pushed the models by applying them to difficult targets, but does not state that the models enabled new ways to modulate those targets.

r003.rationale: The response treats both companies’ commitment across multiple programs as validation, but does not identify an expansion of the Novartis collaboration as evidence of the initial partnership’s success.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re hugely significant for us. They’re an opportunity to bring our AI capabilities together with the deep experience of drug discovery and development at Lilly and Novartis, and apply that combination to real drug discovery problems.

The exciting part is the collaboration: understanding what their teams need, learning from experimental feedback, and using that to guide our models and the molecules we design. That’s how we can start to connect advances in AI with the practical work of developing medicines.

So I see these partnerships as an important step toward our ambition. Ultimately, the measure of success will be whether we can help deliver better medicines to patients.

r001.rationale: The response says the partnerships apply AI to real drug-discovery problems, but does not characterize them as tests of entrenched problems or distinguish them from exploratory trials.

r002.rationale: It mentions guiding models and designing molecules, but does not state that the models enabled new ways to modulate targets researchers had pursued for years.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention an expansion of the Novartis collaboration or interpret one as evidence of success.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re a really important step. The ambition is to use AI to transform drug discovery, and these partnerships give us an opportunity to work on real therapeutic problems alongside teams with deep expertise in developing medicines.

They’re also a test of whether the technology can translate into impact. It’s one thing to build a model with impressive predictive performance; it’s another to use it to help discover a molecule that can ultimately benefit patients. That’s the opportunity here, and there’s still a lot of work to do.

r001.rationale: It calls the partnerships a test of whether the technology can translate into impact and mentions real therapeutic problems, but does not characterize those problems as entrenched or contrast the work with exploratory trials.

r002.rationale: It does not state that Isomorphic Labs’ models enabled new ways to modulate long-pursued targets.

r003.rationale: It does not mention an expansion of the Novartis collaboration or interpret one as evidence of success.
